title: Design a Feed Ranking System
summary: The canonical 'design a feed' case study — integrating ranking, freshness, and diversity into one interview answer.

slides.sectionTitle: Framing the feed as a ranking problem
slides.markdown:
A social feed's job is to **score and order** a pool of candidate posts (from people/pages the user follows, plus recommended content) for each visit. Framed as ML: input is a `(user, candidate post)` pair, output is a relevance score, and the feed shows posts sorted by that score.

The objective isn't "predict if the user will click" alone — most mature feed systems predict several engagement signals (like, comment, share, watch-time, hide/report) and combine them into one final score, since optimizing any single signal in isolation distorts the feed (see the pitfall below).

No feed system scores every possible post for every user with one expensive model. It's a funnel:

![The multi-stage feed ranking pipeline](assets/feed-ranking-pipeline.svg)

**Candidate generation** narrows the entire universe of posts (millions) down to a few hundred plausible ones per user, cheaply. **Ranking** scores that shortlist with a rich, expensive model. **Re-ranking/business rules** applies diversity, freshness, and policy constraints before anything renders. Each stage trades off precision for speed, and each only has to be as accurate as it needs to be to hand a good-enough shortlist to the next stage.

The ranking model draws on three broad feature families:

- **User features** — demographics, long-run interests, recent activity/session behavior.
- **Content features** — post type (text/photo/video), age, author's typical engagement, embeddings of the content itself.
- **Interaction features** — the user's specific history with *this* author or *this* topic, and cross-features like "has this user engaged with this author's last 5 posts."

Cross-features (user × content interactions, not just each side alone) are usually where most of the ranking model's lift actually comes from — they capture "this specific user with this specific content," not just two separate profiles.

You can't directly label "did the user like this post in their heart" — you train on **engagement proxies**: click, like, comment, share, watch-time. Each has a pitfall: clicks reward clickbait, likes under-represent passive-but-genuine interest (lurkers), shares can mean "this is outrageous" as easily as "this is great."

Most production systems predict *multiple* proxies separately, then combine them into a single score with weights tuned against the real business objective (long-run retention, meaningful interactions) — rather than trusting any single proxy to represent the whole picture.

Pure relevance ranking alone tends to over-concentrate: the same author, the same topic, near-duplicate posts back to back. Real feeds layer additional constraints on top of the relevance score (see [ranking-hybrid-recommenders](ranking-hybrid-recommenders) for the general re-ranking pattern):

- **Freshness** — decay a post's score as it ages, so the feed doesn't feel stale.
- **Diversity** — cap how many consecutive posts come from one author or topic cluster.

These are almost always applied as a **re-ranking pass** after relevance scoring, not baked into the relevance model itself — it's much easier to reason about and tune "no more than 2 posts from the same author in the top 10" as an explicit rule than to teach a scoring model that property implicitly.

Feed ranking runs under a tight **latency budget** (typically under a few hundred milliseconds end to end) at massive scale (millions of feed loads per minute). The standard mitigations: **precompute** candidate pools periodically rather than from scratch on every request, **cache** ranked results for a short TTL, and give each pipeline stage its own latency budget so the retrieval stage can't eat the ranking stage's time.

This is exactly why the funnel shape matters for serving, not just accuracy — candidate generation over a two-tower embedding index is fast enough to run per-request, while the heavier ranking model only ever has to run on the couple hundred candidates that stage returns.

Optimizing purely for engagement (clicks, time-on-app) without any counterbalance reliably breeds an **outrage-bait and addictive feedback loop** — content that provokes strong reactions gets amplified regardless of whether it's actually valuable to the user, because the model has no notion of "valuable" beyond the proxy it was given.

The fix mirrors the earlier click-through-rate trap in [ranking-hybrid-recommenders](ranking-hybrid-recommenders): add labels further downstream of the raw engagement signal — surveys on "was this post worth your time," tracking whether engagement predicts long-run retention rather than just the immediate session — and explicitly downweight or filter borderline-policy content regardless of how well it would otherwise score.
